articleTitle: Embedded intelligence supporting predictive asset management in the Energy sector
abstract: In recent years and across a myriad of industries, there has been a realisation that in order to optimise the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of assets and to maintain optimal system level performance whilst assets age and at times with growing and dynamic loading demands, a transition to predictive maintenance from reactive and traditional condition based monitoring and maintenance is required to achieve return of investment (ROI) and performance targets. A sector driven by security and a need to defer investment within the asset base is the Energy sector. After a brief introduction to maintenance process's in the oil and gas domain, this paper presents a novel approach to hierarchical predictive maintenance of assets in through a distributed architecture, represented as domain knowledge-based system, that provides a viable solution for systems containing similar multiple assets.

articleTitle: Clarifying the link between data, diagnosis and Asset Health indices
abstract: Within an asset management framework, such as described by ISO 55000, the role of asset condition and performance analysis is critical to success. An Asset Health Index (AHI) is an asset score which is designed, in some way, to reflect or characterize asset condition and thus likely asset performance in terms of the asset's role. A number of different approaches to generating an AHI have been proposed, and we review several here, including systems which may be: logarithmic, dynamic, weighted, or binary. Each approach has pro's and con's which are demonstrated. For a successful AHI we need to link the available raw data- whether condition monitoring or asset history or maintenance and operational data - through to likely failure modes, or issues which will affect asset performance. We discuss the relevance of particular data sources through to failure modes, and how those can be grouped into logical assessments of an asset or an asset subsystem. Such groupings make sense in terms of users of an AHI system as they deal with, for example, the electrical performance of the dielectric insulation or the thermal performance of the cooling system. Each failure mode can give rise to a likely deterioration rate, which will help direct the actions arising: to gain true value from an AHI, it is necessary to calibrate the scoring system so that similar scores have similar consequent actions and timescales. As examples of the theory and practice of AHI development we look at some individual systems, to demonstrate their practicality, including how they deal with missing data and erroneous or invalid data. Examples are given for power transformer health, focusing on the failure modes related to winding insulation, to bushings and to thermal performance, but always within an overall AHI. In each case we look at the need for an AHI to indicate a condition, and how the owner/operator planned actions and scheduled them. We further discuss the need for calibration of AHI, including both health scoring of the components of a given asset, and between different asset classes. The AHI must provide useful information for intervention: what, and how soon, whether maintenance, refurbishment or planned replacement. This paper has a practical focus, based on real data from users of AHI's in different locations, with different foci on asset performance. Data from analyses, with actions arising and interventions planned are discussed. The integration of AHI into an overall asset management approach, to make sure that the value of an AHI is realized, is presented.

articleTitle: Hydro Ottawa's asset investment planning tool implementation
abstract: Investing to improve aging infrastructure is critical if a utility is going to remain reliable and safe. Like many utilities, Hydro Ottawa built large segments of its distribution system. In recent years, the utility found itself needing to invest in its aging infrastructure at an accelerated pace to improve system reliability and reduce interruptions. The company needed a strategic approach to asset investment planning to achieve its goals. This case study describes how Hydro Ottawa gained corporate sponsorship to implement and deploy the Copperleaf C55 solution, and explains how the company uses C55's Predictive Analytics and Investment Portfolio Optimization capabilities to produce interdependent short- and long-term plans for its projects and programs.

articleTitle: Dynamic maintenance based on criticality in electricity network
abstract: The need to prioritize maintenance activities and investments based on asset criticality and associated risk is seen increasingly as important in industry. However, proper use of criticality in developing maintenance strategies and plans is still at a nascent stage in most organisations. A review of industrial practices showed that criticality is considered as more or less a static quantity that is not updated with sufficient frequency as the operating environment changes. This paper examines an electricity distribution network operator (DNO) to show the need to model the changing nature of criticality and ensure an optimal maintenance strategy and plan, aligned to business needs. A Dynamic Criticality Based Maintenance (DCBM) methodology is proposed to identify factors affecting and influencing changes to criticality, monitor and update asset criticality and exploit the dynamic criticality to optimise maintenance decisions. Asset criticality was calculated using network performance, safety, environmental integrity, maintenance cost among other factors as the consequence categories for asset failure. The criticality for each asset (such as transformer circuit breakers, busbars etc.) is calculated as a weighted sum of the impact of supply loss on each of the consequence categories. Variations in some factors such as electricity demand influences changes in asset criticality with time and therefore criticality is modelled as a dynamic process, which is a function of time in addition to other factors. The performance measure used for the maintenance plan is based on the utility network reliability (quality of service) which is measured in terms of Customer Interruptions (CI) and Customer Minutes Lost (CML). The performance targets (for CIs & CMLs) and standard service levels for DNOs are given in the UK's Office of Gas and Electricity Markets (OFGEM). The results showed evidence of changing asset criticality in the network. The benefit of reviewing maintenance plans based on changing criticality was also highlighted.

articleTitle: Extending SALVO decision-making disciplines into procurement, spares & inventory strategies
abstract: This paper summarises the best practices in decision-making developed by the international SALVO consortium, recently extended to address the optimisation of spares, supply chain and inventory strategies. The paper outlines the problems encountered in such decisions and the disciplines/process that can be used to ensure that the right spares are held in the right numbers. It identifies the factors that need to be taken into account, the cost/risk trade-offs involved, and the process for such decision-making even when available data is limited or unreliable. Applications of these processes have already shown multi-million ££ financial benefits and service level improvements. They have also been successfully used to evaluate alternative supply chain options, the effect of obsolescence on spares strategies, deterioration in storage (`shelf life') and options for distributed or centralised stock holding.

articleTitle: Asset management journey for Dutch light rail system
abstract: The article presents all aspects of asset management for Dutch light rail system including both principles and processes, technical and managerial aspects focusing on tools, standards, data and the application of business processes. The project manager implementation PAS 55 certification, value creation, maintenance planning and training and development are also presented.

articleTitle: If these rails could talk an asset management approach to short text analysis
abstract: The value of tacit knowledge is indispensable in an asset management context, as a full description of an asset or incident can rarely be captured by a set quantitative values. Although we now work in a data rich environment, the limits imposed by quantitative information often result in important asset information being stored as unstructured and unconstrained free text, which can render it impractical to use. This paper is a discussion around extracting information from unstructured data.

articleTitle: Refurbishment or renewal of aging and/or obsolete assets?
abstract: The need and urgency to replace assets, whether by refurbishment or renewal, might depend on a number of contributing factors, such as technical, maintenance, operations, organisational, financial, business and pure risk, reliability and the scope for improvement. Thus all organisational functions might need to contribute to such decisions, which could considerably affect an organisation, either positively or negatively. This paper is based on two case studies of industrial organisations that operate in the same industry with the same control equipment and face similar challenges, yet chose different renewal strategies to suit their particular situations. This paper will cover most of the salient factors that influenced their different asset management renewal strategies.

articleTitle: ISO 55000 in Service provider's context
abstract: ISO 55000-Asset Management Standard in the Service Provider business adds a new dimension to the application of this standard compared to application within an organisation operating its own assets. An Organisation operating its own assets not only has full control of its assets but also the decisions that need to be made around these assets including asset lifecycle strategies, systems, people and processes etc. Because the organisation has control on the interactions that happen around the assets, factors like maturity and capability potential of the organisation do not play a primary role in the `scope' of application of these standards. Even if an organisation outsources Asset Management activities the standards can be applied to a large extent from within the organisation. This Paper looks at case(s) where Asset Management Activities are outsourced to varied degrees and the Service provider tries to establish the Asset Management processes complying to ISO 55000.

articleTitle: Identifying and validating hazards in support of information futureproofing - case study of a building
abstract: The amount of information created and used during lives of infrastructure assets is huge and diverse by nature such as in the form of architectural and structural drawings, structural calculation plans, and operation and maintenance manuals. Such information is typically created by various stakeholders involved in the supply chain. The aim of this paper is to identify and validate hazards of information loss in long term in a case of University building, which can support information futureproofing. A number of interviews were conducted with a UK based key University. The research findings suggest that the hazards of information loss identified by Masood et al [1] are also applicable in a University buildings case and are worth considering in enabling information futureproofing for such infrastructure.

articleTitle: Best practices and challenges in asset management solution implementation
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following: Tata Consultancy Services; enterprise asset management; enterprise information system; integrated asset management services; business value generation; and best practices.

articleTitle: Optimising asset intervention decisions across multiple asset categories at Northern Powergrid
abstract: Over the last decade, Northern Powergrid (NPg) has developed a suite of condition-based risk models to manage their asset risk. However asset managers were limited in their modelling power to determine the right mix of interventions in the asset portfolio, and they wanted to model trade-offs in risk and cost across asset categories. NPg worked with decision-Lab to build an enhanced decision-support tool - the Asset Risk Model (ARM). The ARM can be used to identify, prioritise and optimise interventions within and across multiple and functionally different asset categories to minimise the risk in the portfolio under several budget scenarios.

articleTitle: Delivering a new undergraduate module in Asset Management
abstract: In 2014 the authors presented a paper on the design of a new undergraduate module in Asset Management (AM) as a final year option on a Masters in Engineering (MEng) programme. They undertook to report in 2015 on how the new module was delivered including any challenges, the results, and the students' feedback on its introduction. This paper describes the module's delivery and outcomes. It highlights some of the opportunities for both engagement and improvement of undergraduate teaching of key asset management topics. The paper includes the main lessons learned that need to be factored into undergraduate teaching and engagement in the field of asset management.

articleTitle: Impact on financial performance by physical asset management
abstract: Asset management, as defined in the ISO 55000 standard, enables organizations to realize value from its asset. One of the stated benefits of asset management is increased financial performance. Based on standard financial statement analysis, the paper will explain how asset management on physical assets can improve the financial performance of the organization. The paper will then propose specific measures of asset intensiveness based on data from financial statements. Organizations can use these measures to evaluate the potential impact physical asset management can have on their financial performance. Finally, the paper will present the results of a new survey of asset intensiveness grouped by industry sector. The survey is based on data from all financial statements with end of period in the year 2014 of all Danish companies. In total 187,184 financial statements published in XBRL-format, have been analysed in the survey.

articleTitle: Improving Work Bank prioritisation using Analytical Hierarchical Processing
abstract: This paper presents an implementation of the Analytical Hierarchical Process (AHP) to the process of prioritisation of performing maintenance work orders for track assets. AHP help users to strike a balance between a varied and expanding set of criteria in order to help plan the work. The deployed AHP tool is able to identify the sections of track that should be considered first in order to not only complete the greatest number of work orders but also to potentially reduce the creation of new ones (criteria such as track quality helps to identify sections that are deteriorating faster and therefore generate a larger amount of new work orders). The tool is highly customisable and results can be visualised in a variety of forms, including an interactive web based Geographical Information System (GIS).

articleTitle: A case study on how an enterprise asset management (EAM) system improving the data integrity on fixed asset at PLN Bali Indonesia
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following topics: enterprise asset management system; data integrity; PLN Bali Indonesia; enterprise resources planning software; and electric power distribution unit.

articleTitle: Case study on asset health indices implementation on distribution transformer asset at PLN Bali Indonesia
abstract: This article consists of a collection of slides from the author's conference presentation. Some of the specific areas/topics discussed include: PLN optimising the three conflicting drivers over the distribution transformer asset through a proper combination of interval, inspection method, and mtc method based on asset class, asset categories, and AHI; The mtc methodology based on AHI at PLN has enabled PLN to evaluate its distribution transformer equipment with a more precise data; A tight supervision from PLN holding is required to ensure AHI sustainability to be rolled out to other feeders as monitoring by top management at the business unit is not in place.

articleTitle: Systems modelling of Network Rail's Western Route
abstract: Network Rail's Western Route is undergoing a wide-ranging modernisation programme, with £7.5bn investment in 175 miles of electrification and infrastructure upgrades allowing the introduction of four new fleets of train by 2019. This paper covers the development of a methodology for assessing the capability of the future railway as a system in order to establish whether the upgrade projects, when combined, will achieve the output requirements - which are expressed as train performance.

articleTitle: Trading network risk
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following topics: Great Britain electricity transmission system; power transmission economics; network replacement output incentives; monetising criticality; cost of recovery; and trade-off mechanism.

articleTitle: Risk based integrity management (RBIM)
abstract: RBIM can be applied to all asset types across the organisation to provide a consistent risk management approach. It defines a baseline risk profile and integrity management planning, monitors integrity management plan activities and risk elevators, risk profiles and performance.

articleTitle: Enterprise Risk Management: An improvement journey in nuclear decommissioning
abstract: LLW Repository Ltd is delivering work of strategic national importance, dealing with the UK's low level radioactive waste safely, securely and permanently. LLWR runs Nuclear Decommissioning Authority's National Waste Programme. The company manages the national low level waste repository in Drigg, Cumbria is the UK's only low level radioactive waste disposal facility.

articleTitle: Human behaviours to account for in your service delivery strategies
abstract: The article presents how human behavior accounts in the service delivery strategies. It presents challenges and opportunities on how service are delivered.

articleTitle: Bridge Asset Management in Hertfordshire - now and in the future
abstract: Highway Infrastructure is a strategic national asset including more than 300,000 bridges. The majority are owned by organisations struggling to deliver their duties and obligations under increasing budget pressures. Hertfordshire County Council is using Asset Management to better understand its bridge stock both now and in the future, and to provide efficiency in maintenance and management of the stock. Hertfordshire's bridges range from medieval arches to modern steel composite structures, from small brick culverts to modern post-tensioned concrete viaducts. These bridges carry both the strategic primary road network and the local road network. The Department for Transport promotes adoption of Asset Management, with future funding being linked to the level of embedment within the Local Authority. Our approach in Hertfordshire aims to achieve long-term performance in service levels, resilience, budget certainty and efficiency within an environment of increasing traffic, climate change and ageing infrastructure. Data is the bedrock of asset management. Inventory and condition data have been collected for many years, and a GIS based bridge management system supports effective management of the stock. Tools based on nationally agreed deterioration and cost models facilitate prioritisation and long-term scenario planning. Maintenance activities are targeted at achieving long-term benefit to the network, maintaining service levels whilst minimising whole life costs. Key priorities include maintaining essential protective elements such as movement joints and paint systems, and effective repair of deteriorated concrete bridges is critical. There are exciting technological developments in automated bridge inspection and photogrammetry which we are trialling, and which we expect to positively impact on our bridge stock management. National initiatives include research on implementation of BIM in Asset Management, better understanding of bridge deterioration and development of a National Bridge Condition Reporting methodology.

articleTitle: Case study: How smart tagging of water assets delivers benefits to customers and utilities
abstract: This case study looks at the deployment of the OXEMS Underground Asset Management System during commercial trials carried out with a UK Water Company (UKWC) during 2013 and 2014. The case study looks in particular at a part of these trials undertaken as part of a rehab scheme in the Midlands. The ultimate aims of the trial were to collect operational data and to demonstrate rapid ROI.

articleTitle: Integrated Asset Management as a Business Management System
abstract: An innovative approach taken to integrate all our management systems under the umbrella of the PAS 55 certified Asset Management System. Health & Safety, Environment and Asset Engineering teams work together to produce a central system that is scalable to work for all power stations; efficiently, effectively and compliantly.

articleTitle: Assessing smart grid interventions for future power networks
abstract: The aim of this study is to assess the suitability and cost-effectiveness of novel techniques along with traditional reinforcements for electricity distribution networks, in order to analyse expected investments up to 2050 under DECC (Department of Energy and Climate Change) scenarios. These smart techniques are evaluated under different demand scenarios to assist decision makers in future power networks planning. The evaluation of assets planning is based on the LCNF Tier 2 FALCON (Flexible Approaches for Low Carbon Optimised Networks) project network. The area of study is Milton Keynes (East Midlands), being composed of six 11kV primaries. To undertake this analysis is used a revolutionary new software tool for electricity distribution network planning, called Scenario Investment Model (SIM). Once results have been obtained a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) is performed, to propose an optimal solution for assets investments. In this context, this study summarises the benefit of novel techniques versus traditional reinforcements for long-term planning, highlighting the value for money and the criteria related for investment planning.

articleTitle: Asset management, systems and information systems
abstract: Presents a compilation of slides covering the following: information systems; asset management business system; conceptual thinking; Dunning-Kruger effect; systems thinking; and technology obsolescence management system.

articleTitle: The asset information Maturity Model
abstract: Information is one of the most vital strategic assets any organization possesses. The article presents and overview of the asset information maturity model which includes advanced analytics, information analysis, information collaboration, data standardization and baseline assessment.

articleTitle: Counting the cost of criticality
abstract: This article consists of a collection of slides from the author's conference presentation. Some of the specific areas/topics discussed include: Great Britain electricity transmission system; criticality index; criticality monetisation; high impact low probability events; and trading mechanism.

articleTitle: A Toolkit for structures Asset Management
abstract: Maintaining infrastructure is challenging for asset owners, who make complex decisions on investment planning and prioritisation of maintenance spending. The use of tools to analyse data provides a repeatable and auditable evidence base to support decision making. The Structures Investment Toolkit (SIT) is a decision support tool that was developed by Atkins to enable Highways England to carry out lifecycle planning on their structures asset. SIT is one of the few tools that performs calculations at element level, taking into account external factors (environment, traffic levels, etc.) as well as the condition of other elements within a structure to estimate the rate of deterioration.

articleTitle: Comprehensive asset management in offshore wind with ISO 55000
abstract: This article consists of a collection of slides from the author's conference presentation. Some of the specific areas/topics discussed include: DONG energy wind power; offshore wind farms; business operations; operations maturity level; AIM programme; AIM wheel drives standardisation; WP operations maturity; asset management system; and ISO 55001 standard compliance.

articleTitle: Asset management e-learning in the highways sector
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following: asset management; e-learning; and highway sector.

articleTitle: Decision support tool: Driving the asset management transformation on the M25
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following topics: decision support tool; asset management transformation; asset management strategy; M25 DBFO contract; and motorway construction.

articleTitle: How asset managers can achieve a step change in performance
abstract: Presents a collection of slides covering the following: asset management; investment; cost-down methods; cost-down maturity growth; and CAPEX.

articleTitle: Automatic real-time fault detection for industrial assets using metasensors
abstract: Large-scale industrial plants require physical sensors to continuously measure quantities such as temperatures or pressures. A large number of sensors is required to accurately describe the operating state of the plant, which unfortunately makes it very difficult for them to be effectively monitored by human operators. In this work we present a method to construct so-called metasensors, virtual sensors that compress the information from several sensors in an optimal manner. These metasensors are used as inputs to a novel anomaly detection system that automatically alerts operators to abnormal operation behaviour.

articleTitle: Drinking Water Safety Plan DWSP
abstract: The most effective means of consistently ensuring the safety of a drinking water supply is through the use of a comprehensive risk assessment and risk management approach that encompasses all steps in water supply from catchment to consumer. In these guidelines, such approaches are called water safety plans.

articleTitle: Understanding the context of the organisation: Adopting a systems thinking approach to asset management
abstract: The article presents Highways England road investment strategy. A value improvement model for Highways England asset management which adopts a whole life cost approach is also presented.

articleTitle: Valuing the wider benefits of road maintenance funding
abstract: A new analysis tool has been developed by TRL, on behalf of the Department for Transport, to help assess the user and other impacts of maintenance as well as the direct maintenance works costs. This new tool has been developed in line with a recognised asset management view of the assessment of road maintenance. Studies for roads in Scotland, by Transport Scotland and local roads in England, by the RAC Foundation with ADEPT, have recognised that the impacts of maintenance funding levels are wider than the direct works costs and the costs of disruption to road users. This work uses the change in the condition of the road network over time under different spending trajectories to assess the impacts on the wider costs to society in relation to future maintenance activity. Currently, not all effects can be quantified but the aim with the new tool is to enable users to consider a wide range of potential impacts resulting from the changes in carriageway conditions and the maintenance works undertaken on the network under different funding levels and maintenance policies. Preliminary analyses using the tool for local roads in England (excluding London) have shown the suitability and flexibility of the tool.

articleTitle: Engineering towards a resilient world-managing client expectations
abstract: Traditionally, extreme events were predominantly considered for structures where there was a high probability of such occurrence, due to their type and location, or if their failure would have a significantly major consequence, such as offshore structures or nuclear reactors. Such clients are knowledgeable and confident in defining the event parameters and the performance requirements of their structures both during and just after hazard events. This is based on a rigorous understanding of risk, consequence and the costs associated with lack of resilience and post event clean up. Stakeholders and clients fresh to the subject can struggle to assess the criticality of their asset and set appropriate design requirements for extreme events such as earthquake, flood, extended fire and explosion, without understanding the subtleties of designing for resilience. Neglecting to engage with this at project inception, before design requirements are determined and procurement is initiated, can lead to unrealistic or caveated tender returns and ultimately fail to achieve a resilient infrastructure solution.

articleTitle: Key performance indicators for cantonal road management in Switzerland
abstract: With respect to renewal maintenance of road networks it is often desired to have indicators of the sufficiency of the amount of maintenance being done and the efficiency of the maintenance interventions being carried out, herein referred to maintenance sufficiency and cost efficiency respectively. The creation of such indicators is challenging. In this article, steps to create such indicators are discussed and an initial set of implementable indicators for Swiss cantons is proposed. The indicators discussed were developed with the support of a group of Swiss cantons [1]. The further steps needed to develop a final set of indicators are listed.
